# Architecture Description

> Architecture Description · 20 sections [loom:reference-model=core-architecture@1.0 2026-09-24T23:24:47.911Z youna.shin@ucdenver.edu]

# Executive Summary

*Summarise the solution, the problem it solves, and the two or three decisions that most shape it — in language a non-technical sponsor can act on. Write this section last and keep it under a page. Its job is to let a reader who will never open the rest of the document know what was decided and what it commits the organisation to.*

# Problem Statement and Business Context

*State the business problem in terms of the outcome that is currently not being achieved, and the drivers, constraints and deadlines that bound any acceptable answer. Name the business capabilities this solution supports so the work can be traced to the capability model rather than justified on its own terms. A problem statement that could describe any project is not yet a problem statement.*

> **Recommended models:** ArchiMate Motivation View · Capability Map

# Stakeholder Analysis

*Identify who has power over this solution, who has interest in it, and who has both — and for each, the specific concern they will judge it by. Then point at the section of this document that answers each concern. A stakeholder whose concern is not answered anywhere is either out of scope or a gap, and it is much cheaper to decide which now.*

> **Recommended models:** Power-Interest Grid

# Context

*Draw the boundary. State plainly what is inside this solution and what is outside it, name every external actor and system that crosses that boundary, and say what flows across each crossing. Then record the technology stack decisions that the boundary implies, with the reasoning attached. This section matters because scope disagreement is the most expensive kind: it surfaces late, as integration failure or as work nobody agreed to fund, and every later section in this document is only as trustworthy as the boundary drawn here.*

> **Recommended models:** BTABoK Context Diagram · ArchiMate Application Layer View · C4 Context Diagram · ArchiMate Technology Layer View · UML Use Case Diagram · Benefits Realization Canvas

> **BTABoK concerns:** C01.01 Context Model · C01.02 External Integration Boundary · C01.03 Benefits Realization

# Functional Decomposition

*Decompose the solution into elements that each have one clear responsibility, and name the interface each element offers to the others. Show at least one end-to-end scenario tracing a real request through those elements, because a decomposition that has never been walked through a scenario usually hides a missing element or a circular dependency. Keep the decomposition traceable in both directions: every element should answer to a requirement, and every requirement should land on an element.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Component Diagram · C4 Component Diagram · ArchiMate Application Layer View · Bounded Context Map · API Contract Specification · UML Sequence Diagram · EventStorming — Design Level · BPMN Business Process Diagram · UML Activity Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C02.01 Functional Decomposition · C02.02 Interface Definition · C02.03 Interaction Scenario · C02.04 Process Analysis · C02.06 Bounded Context Design

# Usability and Accessibility

*Describe how users move through this solution and what the system does at each step to keep them oriented — how it confirms, how it warns, and how it lets someone recover from a mistake. State the accessibility conformance level as a commitment with a testing method behind it, not as an intention. The shape of the interface API, the scope of the design system, and the error contract are architectural decisions with user-experience consequences, and they belong here rather than being settled implicitly during implementation.*

> **Recommended models:** Lo-Fi Wireframe, annotated · User Journey Map · Compliance Matrix

> **BTABoK concerns:** C15.01 Interaction Model · C15.02 Accessibility Design

# Information Model

*Define the entities this solution stores and processes, their relationships and cardinality, and — the part most documents skip — who owns each one. Ownership is an architectural decision, not an administrative one: an entity with two writers and no named owner will drift, and reconciling it later costs more than designing it now. Show how information moves as well as how it is shaped, and state where regulated or personal data enters the picture, because that determines constraints in the Security, Safety and Deployment sections.*

> **Recommended models:** Entity-Relationship Diagram · UML Class Diagram · Aggregate Design Canvas · Data Flow Diagram · UML Sequence Diagram · RACI Chart · Authority Matrix · UML State Machine Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C03.01 Logical Data Model · C03.02 Information Flow Model · C03.03 Data Ownership Model · C03.09 Entity Lifecycle Model

# Integration Architecture

*Map every connection this solution makes to another system and name the pattern each one uses — synchronous request, published event, batch file, shared store. For each connection state the contract, who owns it, and how it is versioned, because an unversioned contract is a future outage with a date on it. Say what happens when the far side is slow, wrong, or absent; integration sections that document only the happy path are the most common cause of production surprise.*

> **Recommended models:** ArchiMate Application Layer View · C4 Context Diagram · Data Flow Diagram · Bounded Context Map · API Contract Specification · UML Component Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C09.01 Integration Topology · C09.03 API Contract Design

# Concurrency and Execution Model

*Describe what actually runs at the same time — processes, threads, workers, consumers — and where any two of them touch the same state. For each shared-state touchpoint, name the control that makes it safe, and for each message path, state the ordering and delivery guarantee you rely on. Concurrency defects are the hardest class of defect to reproduce and the most expensive to find in production, so the value of this section is precisely that it forces the guarantees to be written down before they are assumed.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Activity Diagram · UML Component Diagram · EventStorming — Process Level · UML State Machine Diagram · UML Sequence Diagram · Aggregate Design Canvas · Enterprise Integration Patterns

> **BTABoK concerns:** C07.01 Process and Thread Structure · C07.03 Concurrency Control Design · C07.04 Message Ordering Design

# Deployment Topology

*Place every runtime component on the infrastructure that hosts it — nodes, zones, regions, environments — and show the network zones between them. State the high-availability and disaster-recovery design explicitly, with the redundancy that supports it and the RPO and RTO it is sized to meet. Describe how dev, test and production differ, because undocumented environment drift is where 'it worked in staging' comes from.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Deployment Diagram · C4 Deployment Diagram · ArchiMate Technology Layer View · Trust Zone Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C04.01 Deployment Topology · C04.02 Network Zone Design · C04.03 HA/DR Design

# Security Architecture

*Enumerate the attack surface — every entry point an outside party can reach — and run a structured threat analysis over it rather than listing controls you already intended to build. Define the trust zones and say what changes when data crosses between them. Then state the identity and access model and how data is protected at rest and in transit. Security is the most heavily regulated architectural concern; this section is the one most likely to be read by someone outside the delivery team, so make the reasoning legible, not just the conclusion.*

*For a public web product, treat the browser as hostile territory: cover session handling, token storage, CSRF and XSS exposure, and the content security policy alongside the server-side controls. The attack surface includes everything your JavaScript can reach.*

> **Recommended models:** STRIDE Threat Model · Attack Tree · Trust Zone Diagram · Data Flow Diagram · Access Control Matrix · UML Sequence Diagram · Entity-Relationship Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C05.01 Attack Surface Map · C05.02 Trust Zone Design · C05.03 Identity and Access Model · C05.04 Data Protection Design

# Safety and Hazard Analysis

*Safety is not security. Security asks what a hostile actor could do; safety asks what this system could do wrong on its own — a payment taken twice, an audit trail silently truncated, a decision applied to the wrong record. Identify those hazards systematically, state the operational constraints that bound them, and describe the fail-safe behaviour for each: what the system does when it cannot proceed correctly. Say how each control is tested, because an untested fail-safe is an assumption.*

> **Recommended models:** Hazard and Operability Study · UML State Machine Diagram · UML Sequence Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C16.01 Safety Hazard Model · C16.02 Operational Constraints · C16.03 Fail-Safe Design

# Reliability and Failure Design

*State the availability target as a number with an error budget attached, not as an adjective. Then work the failure modes: for each component, what can fail, what the user sees when it does, how it is detected, and what recovers it. Size redundancy to the stated target rather than to convention, and describe how recovery has actually been exercised. Without this section, real availability characteristics stay unknown until an incident reveals them.*

> **Recommended models:** Quality Attribute Scenario · SLO / Error Budget Table · Failure Mode and Effects Analysis · UML State Machine Diagram · UML Deployment Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C13.01 Reliability Targets and Error Budget · C13.02 Failure Mode Analysis · C13.03 Redundancy and Replication Model · C13.04 Recovery Design

# Performance

*Write performance requirements as scenarios with numbers: this stimulus, under this load, produces this response within this measure. Allocate the budget hop by hop so that each component knows its share, and name the constraint you believe binds first — the component that will saturate before anything else. Define the validation gate that must pass before release. Performance targets stated as adjectives cannot be designed against and cannot be tested.*

*Express user-facing targets in the terms users actually experience — time to first meaningful render, interaction latency, and behaviour on a slow or intermittent connection — not only server-side response times. State the device and network baseline you are designing for.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Sequence Diagram · Quality Attribute Scenario · Latency Budget · User Journey Map

> **BTABoK concerns:** C10.01 Performance Scenario · C10.02 Latency Budget

# Operational Design

*Describe how this solution will be seen once it is running: which metrics, logs, traces and alerts exist, on which components, and what each alert means someone should do. Describe the pipeline that carries a change from commit to production, including the gates it must pass. Operability designed after the fact becomes the delivery team's permanent tax, so treat the signals and the pipeline as architecture, not as implementation detail.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Deployment Diagram · C4 Container Diagram · UML State Machine Diagram · Pipeline Diagram · BPMN Business Process Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C06.01 Observability Model · C06.02 Availability and Recovery Design · C06.03 Deployment Pipeline Design

# Operations and Release Governance

*This section sits above the operational design and covers what people do with it. Define the release and change process — how a change is approved, rolled out, and rolled back — and the SLO governance that decides when to stop shipping features and spend the error budget on stability instead. State who is accountable during an incident and what the readiness gate is that a new service must pass before it is allowed to take production traffic.*

> **Recommended models:** Pipeline Diagram · BPMN Business Process Diagram · Compliance Matrix

> **BTABoK concerns:** C12.03 Release and Change Process · C12.05 SLA/SLO Governance

# Maintainability and Evolvability

*State the coupling rules this solution is designed to hold — which modules may depend on which, and which dependencies are forbidden — and how those rules are enforced automatically rather than by review. Describe the test architecture: what is tested at which level, and what makes each level possible. Name the technical debt you are knowingly taking on and the condition under which it gets paid. Maintainability is the cost of every future change compounded; this section is where that cost is made visible while it can still be influenced.*

> **Recommended models:** UML Package Diagram · UML Component Diagram

> **BTABoK concerns:** C14.01 Modularity and Coupling Model · C14.03 Testability Design

# Architecture Decisions

*Record each significant decision as its own entry: the context that forced a choice, the options considered, what was chosen, and what the choice costs. The options not taken are the most valuable part — they are what stops the decision being relitigated in six months by someone who cannot see why it was made.*

> **Recommended models:** Architecture Decision Record

# Risks and Mitigations

*List the architectural risks with likelihood and impact, the mitigation for each, and the person accountable for it. Distinguish risks you are mitigating from risks you are accepting, and say why the accepted ones are acceptable. An unowned risk is a wish.*

> **Recommended models:** Threat / Opportunity Matrix

# Roadmap and Transition

*Show how the solution reaches its target state in stages, what each stage delivers on its own, and what depends on what. Include the transitional states explicitly — the periods where old and new run together are usually where the real complexity and the real risk sit.*

> **Recommended models:** ArchiMate Migration View · OKR Trace Map
